steps.say: The practice kitchen. Some things at home can make you poorly if you drink them, eat them or get them on your skin. Let's find them.

lines.bleach: Bleach: a warning sign. Never touch it.
lines.oven_cleaner: Oven cleaner: a warning sign. Only for grown-ups.
lines.washing_tabs: Washing tablets look like sweets, but they're not food.
lines.drain_cleaner: Drain cleaner: a warning sign. Never touch it.

steps.say: Find the 4 things with a warning sign: a red diamond.
steps.done: You found them all!

lines.juice_cleaner: A cleaner in a juice bottle! Chemicals belong in their own bottles, so tell a grown-up.

steps.say: Never touch them: tell a grown-up. Touch Gus.
steps.done: Gus puts them up high, in the locked cupboard.

steps.say: These look like sweets, but they are medicine. Who gives you medicine?

steps.say: A tiny round battery is on the floor. What do you do?

choices.why: Never put a battery in your mouth. Give it to a grown-up.

choices.text: Give it to the baby to play with
choices.why: Babies put things in their mouths. Give it to a grown-up.

steps.done: Grown-ups put button batteries away safely.

steps.say: Red berries in the garden look yummy. Do you eat them?

choices.text: No: only food a grown-up gives me

choices.why: Some berries and mushrooms make you poorly. Never eat them from outside.

steps.done: Never eat wild berries or mushrooms.

name_it.title: Danger at home
lines: A warning sign means: don't touch, tell a grown-up.
Cleaners and medicines live up high, locked away.
Medicine only from your own grown-up.
Batteries go to a grown-up, never in your mouth.
Never eat wild berries or mushrooms.
name_it.source: The WHO, poison centres and the Child Accident Prevention Trust

little.try_real: With a grown-up: find the warning signs on bottles at home, and check they live up high, locked away.

sources.fact: Keep medicines, cleaners and chemicals out of children's reach and sight, locked away, in their own containers.
Button batteries are dangerous if swallowed; keep them away from children and give loose ones to a grown-up.
sources.source: Child Accident Prevention Trust, button batteries

sources.fact: Liquid laundry and washing tablets look like sweets; keep them up high and closed.
Medicines only from a trusted grown-up, the right dose; never call medicine sweets.

steps.say: The practice kitchen and garage. Today: the warning signs, the child lock, and why cleaners are never mixed.

lines.sym_corrosive: Corrosive: it can hurt skin and eyes.
lines.sym_toxic: Toxic: very dangerous if swallowed, breathed in or on the skin.
lines.sym_harmful: Harmful, the exclamation mark: it can make you poorly or sore.

steps.say: Find the 4 warning signs. Each red diamond means something different.
steps.done: You know the warning signs!

safe_mistake.why: Some cleaners make a harmful gas when they are mixed, like bleach with other cleaners. It can hurt your eyes and lungs.
safe_mistake.right: Never mix cleaners. Ask a grown-up: they use one at a time, with the window open.

steps.say: Mo says: 'Let's pour the bleach and the toilet cleaner into the bucket together, for a super cleaner!' What do you do?
steps.done: Tell a grown-up: never mix cleaners.

steps.say: The practice garage. Find the 3 things that should be locked away up high.

steps.say: Your friend has a headache tablet for you. Do you take it?

choices.text: No: medicine only from my own grown-up

choices.why: Even one can be wrong for you. Only your own grown-up gives you medicine.

name_it.title: The poisons cupboard
lines: Learn the warning signs: corrosive, toxic, flammable, harmful.
Cleaners and medicines up high, the child lock clicked shut.
Never mix cleaners: some make a harmful gas.
A swallowed button battery is an emergency: call {number}.
Never eat wild mushrooms or berries.
name_it.source: The UN's Globally Harmonized System of warning signs, the WHO, poison centres and the Child Accident Prevention Trust

middle.try_real: With a grown-up: look for the warning signs on the bottles at home, check the child locks click, and find your country's poison centre number together.

sources.fact: The red-diamond warning signs (pictograms) of the UN's Globally Harmonized System: corrosive, toxic (the skull), flammable (the flame), harmful or irritant (the exclamation mark) and more.
Never mix cleaning products: bleach with ammonia or with acids (some toilet cleaners) makes toxic gases.
sources.source: US CDC, cleaning and disinfecting safely

sources.fact: A swallowed button battery is an emergency: it can cause serious harm inside within two hours; get medical help straight away.
sources.source: Child Accident Prevention Trust, button batteries

sources.fact: Never eat wild mushrooms or berries unless an expert has said they are safe; poisonous ones can look like edible ones.
Child-resistant locks and keeping products in their original, labelled containers prevent poisonings.
sources.source: WHO, World report on child injury prevention (2008), poisoning

big.twist: Someone says 'it's just the battery', and nothing glows.

steps.say: The practice house. Today: carbon monoxide, cleaners, button batteries and medicine.
This is a carbon monoxide alarm. Carbon monoxide (CO) is a gas you can't see, smell or taste. It can come from a faulty boiler, cooker or fire.
Grown-ups test it every month: press and hold the test button until it beeps.
steps.done: Beep beep: it works.

steps.say: Practice: it's night, and the CO alarm is sounding.
The CO alarm is sounding. What do you do?

choices.text: Wake everyone and get out into fresh air
Turn it off and go back to bed
choices.why: Never ignore it: you can't see or smell CO. Get everyone out.
Get out first. The fire service or a gas engineer makes it safe.

steps.done: Everyone out, into fresh air.

choices.text: Get everyone out anyway, and call {number}

steps.done: Treat every alarm as real: everyone out.

safe_mistake.right: One cleaner at a time, the window open, rinse between, and read the label first.

name_it.title: Poisons and gases
lines: CO can't be seen or smelt: the alarm warns you. Test it every month.
The alarm sounds: everyone out, call {number} from outside.
Never mix cleaners: one at a time, the window open.
A swallowed button battery: call {number} straight away.
Medicine: only the label's amount, from a grown-up.
name_it.source: The NHS, the US CDC, the WHO, poison centres and the Child Accident Prevention Trust

big.try_real: With a grown-up: find your CO alarm (or talk about getting one), press its test button together, and save your poison centre's number.

sources.fact: Carbon monoxide has no colour, smell or taste; it comes from faulty boilers, cookers, fires and engines; a CO alarm warns you.
If your CO alarm sounds: leave the home straight away, get into fresh air, call the emergency number from outside, and stay out until someone says it's safe.
sources.source: US CDC, carbon monoxide poisoning prevention

sources.fact: Test CO alarms regularly (monthly) and replace them as the maker says.
sources.source: US Consumer Product Safety Commission, carbon monoxide

sources.fact: Never mix bleach with ammonia or acids (some toilet cleaners): it makes chloramine or chlorine gas.
sources.source: US CDC, cleaning and disinfecting safely

sources.fact: A swallowed button battery needs emergency help straight away; don't make the child sick; take the packet.
sources.source: Child Accident Prevention Trust, button batteries
